in_text_mentions: The child (II-2) (Fig. 2a) is the first male child of apparently healthy nonconsanguineous parents. The mother and the father were 33 and 45 years old respectively at the time of his birth. Fetal movements were poor. Routine ultrasound examination was normal until 23 weeks of gestation when bilateral radial agenesis was demonstrated. The child was born post-term at 43 weeks of gestation by normal vaginal delivery. Birth weight was 2810 g (10th-25th centile). He was admitted to our institute at 4 months of age. Physical examination showed good nutritional status, forehead and right cheek telang

of gestation, suggesting the presence of upper limb anomalies. This finding was confirmed at 15th week of gestation. The couple opted for termination of pregnancy. The chromosomal analysis of amniotic cells (400 bands) excluded any visible abnormality. Post-mortem examination of the fetus demonstrated bilateral radial agenesis (Fig. 2b). The mother had a previous pregnancy, which ended in spontaneous abortion at the 2nd month of gestation (II-1). There was no exposure to alcohol, smoking or infections during pregnancy. A subsequent pregnancy resulted in the delivery of a healthy child (II-4).

panels.rationale: Clinical photograph of a newborn's upper limb showing forearm shortening and internal rotation of the hand, consistent with radial clubhand deformity in TAR syndrome. The article title ('Thrombocytopenia-absent radius syndrome: prenatal diagnosis of a rare syndrome') and in-text mentions ('Physical examination revealed deformity of the upper limbs') confirm TAR syndrome diagnosis. The caption labels this as an 'ultrasound image' but the image is clearly a clinical photograph with overlaid arrows. Skin tone cannot be assessed from the grayscale image.

in_text_mentions: Follow-up ultrasound scans were performed every four weeks. At 31 weeks, the mother went into preterm labor, evolving to normal delivery without complications. The newborn developed respiratory distress, requiring endotracheal intubation and mechanical ventilation. Physical examination revealed deformity of the upper limbs, without other anatomical changes (Figure 2). On the sixth day of life, the ventilation patterns worsened and the infant developed pneumothorax, subsequently evolving to death.

A: Fetal ultrasound at 21 weeks in a case of TAR syndrome; caption explicitly states absence of radii and shortening of the ulnae, the hallmark skeletal manifestations of TAR. Real patient imaging, no third-party restriction. B: Fetal ultrasound sagittal view showing internally rotated hands in a fetus with TAR syndrome; consistent with the radial deviation/clubhand spectrum of TAR. Real patient imaging; internally rotated hands is a recognized but less commonly emphasized manifestation, hence variant.

plate_findings.evidence: Diminutive second and third metacarpal bones of the left hand; bowed ulna (visual)

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 2 panels (A, B). A: Radiograph of right upper extremity showing absent radius in a patient with TAR syndrome, labeled 'Absent radii (right)'.
